analysis.one_liner: Limits natural gas trading and penalizes price gouging during federally declared emergencies.
analysis.headline: Introduced with a single cosponsor, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died in the House Agriculture Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to write rules requiring natural gas trading facilities to impose trading limits during a federally declared emergency, to prevent market distortions. It would also make it a violation, punishable by a fine of up to $1 million per day, to sell natural gas on the spot or day-ahead market during an emergency at a price above a baseline the Commission sets. Finally, it would order a study of who profited from the natural gas price spikes during Winter Storm Uri, the 2021 Texas freeze.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that buy natural gas and electricity during a federally declared emergency, when prices on spot and day-ahead markets have historically spiked — as they did during the 2021 Texas winter storm, when gas prices soared and utility bills exploded.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Natural gas and electricity customers in emergencies

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CFTC to write rules mandating trading limits on natural gas spot and day-ahead markets during a federally declared emergency, to prevent market distortions.
Creates a penalty of up to $1 million per day for selling or offering natural gas on the spot or day-ahead market during an emergency at prices above a Commission-set baseline.
Requires a CFTC study and report to Congress, within 180 days, on who benefitted from the dramatic natural gas price increases during Winter Storm Uri, with recommendations for future emergencies.

analysis.who_pays: Natural gas traders and marketers who profit from emergency price spikes; the bill would cap their trading and expose them to fines up to $1 million per day for excessive pricing during declared emergencies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Natural gas traders profiting from price spikes

drawbacks.text: The bill applies only during emergencies declared by a federal agency or instrumentality, so it would not cover price spikes like Winter Storm Uri unless a federal emergency had been declared; state-declared emergencies alone would not trigger it.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has limited authority over physical spot markets, so giving it power to set price baselines and limit spot-market trading would be a significant and legally uncertain expansion of its jurisdiction.

Capping prices during an emergency can have side effects: if suppliers or traders expect to be penalized for selling above a baseline, some may hold gas back rather than sell into a shortage, potentially making supply tighter during a crisis. The bill directed a study of the Uri price spikes precisely because the underlying market behavior was not well understood.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real and costly problem — gas and electricity prices in Texas during Winter Storm Uri produced enormous bills for ordinary households and billions in losses. Its protections, however, were narrow: they trigger only on a federal emergency declaration, and the penalties and trading limits were untested in a market the CFTC does not traditionally supervise. As written it was a modest consumer safeguard rather than a comprehensive fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joaquin Castro of Texas introduced the bill on October 27, 2021, for himself and Rep. Lloyd Doggett, in the aftermath of Winter Storm Uri's natural gas price spikes.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture on the day of introduction, and about a month later was referred to the Subcommittee on Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Natural gas traders and marketers who profit from emergency price spikes are better off; nothing was done to limit that trading or to reveal who gained during Winter Storm Uri, and the study the bill ordered never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gas traders profiting from emergency price spikes

for.name: Rep. Joaquin Castro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in response to Winter Storm Uri's natural gas price spikes and referred it to committee.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. David Scott (D-GA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's only support was its two Texas Democratic sponsors, and no member or group publicly opposed it, so no partisan split shows in the record.

industries.industry: Natural gas traders and marketers on spot and day-ahead markets
industries.note: These traders captured the windfall from emergency price spikes like Winter Storm Uri's, when gas sold for hundreds of times normal prices. The bill would have capped their trading during federally declared emergencies and exposed excessive pricing to fines up to $1 million per day, and its study would have publicly identified who profited.

Producers and regulated utilities sell the gas, so emergency price caps cut both ways for them — they could lose windfall revenue but also face more predictable prices and fewer distortions when buying fuel during a crisis.
